text: As fire sets brushwood ablaze and makes water boil, come down to make your name known to your enemies, so that the nations tremble before you.

versions.text: As fire sets brushwood ablaze and makes the water boil, come down to make your name known to your enemies, so that the nations tremble before you.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has no article on מַיִם ('water'), so the generic 'water' reads better than 'the water'. Also, the imperative 'come down' has no verb behind it in this verse; it is carried over from the plea at the end of the preceding chapter. Consider a brief footnote such as: 'The words "come down" continue the plea of the previous verse in the Hebrew text.'

text: When you did awesome things we did not look for, you came down, and the mountains melted away before you.

versions.text: When you did awesome things we did not look for, you came down, and the mountains quaked before you.
versions.explanation: The verb נָזֹלּוּ means 'flowed down, melted, streamed', not 'quaked' (which would be a different root, e.g. רגז in v. 1). 'Melted away' preserves the imagery and avoids duplicating the trembling motif of v. 1.

text: From ages past no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God but you, who acts for the one who waits for him.
You come to those who gladly do what is right, who remember you in your ways. But you were angry, for we went on sinning; in our sins we have lived a long time—can we still be saved?

versions.text: You meet the one who gladly does what is right, those who remember you in your ways. But you were angry, for we went on sinning; in our sins we have lived a long time—can we still be saved?
versions.explanation: The current wording shifts from singular ('the one who') to plural ('those who') within one clause, which stumbles when read aloud. Using consistent plural forms matches the plural verb יִזְכְּרוּךָ and flows more naturally.

text: We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a filthy garment. We all wither like a leaf, and our sins sweep us away like the wind.
No one calls on your name or rouses himself to take hold of you, for you have hidden your face from us and made us waste away in the grip of our sins.
Yet, LORD, you are our Father. We are the clay, and you are the potter; we are all the work of your hand.
Do not be angry beyond measure, LORD; do not remember our sin forever. Look upon us, we pray: we are all your people.
Your holy cities have become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation.
Our holy and glorious house, where our fathers praised you, has been burned with fire, and all that we treasured lies in ruins.
After all this, LORD, will you hold back? Will you keep silent and afflict us beyond measure?
